[PATH:empirical] Quarterly, city-level panel data on minimum wage changes and unemployment claims from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (e.g., Local Area Unemployment Statistics), focusing on low-wage industries (retail, hospitality) and comparing Q1 versus other-quarter implementations. — Directly tests the temporal qualifier by leveraging variation in the timing of state and city minimum wage increases within urban U.S. labor markets, allowing estimation of short-run unemployment effects with high-frequency data.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching models with seasonal hiring and firing patterns (e.g., DMP framework extended to include calendar-quarter effects and minimum wage shocks), calibrated to U.S. urban low-wage labor markets. — Explores the mechanism through which Q1 implementation may amplify unemployment fluctuations, e.g., by coinciding with post-holiday layoffs or seasonal hiring frictions, providing a causal structure to interpret empirical findings.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis or systematic review of existing studies on minimum wage timing and employment effects, focusing on studies that separately estimate impacts by quarter of implementation or control for seasonal adjustment. — Synthesizes prior evidence to assess whether the disputed timing effect is consistently observed across contexts, and identifies gaps or methodological issues (e.g., publication bias, data frequency) that could explain the current 0.5 confidence level.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with high turnover

qualifier.temporal: when implemented during the first quarter of the calendar year
qualifier.geographic: within urban labor markets in the United States

[PATH:empirical] Quarterly Workforce Indicators (QWI) data from the U.S. Census Bureau, merged with state-level minimum wage changes during the 2008-2009 recession — High-frequency, geographically granular data on employment flows in low-wage, high-turnover urban sectors can reveal whether minimum wage increases timed during recessions amplify short-run unemployment fluctuations compared to increases during expansions.

[PATH:empirical] Event-study analysis of city-level minimum wage ordinances passed during recessionary periods (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco) using synthetic control methods — Comparing unemployment dynamics in cities that raised minimum wages during a recession to matched cities that did not, focusing on short-run (quarterly) fluctuations, directly tests the hypothesis in the specified scope.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching labor market models with endogenous timing of wage floors and aggregate demand shocks — A calibrated model can isolate the causal mechanism: if minimum wage increases are implemented when labor demand is already falling, the resulting mismatch between wage costs and firm hiring may exacerbate cyclical unemployment volatility in high-turnover sectors.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies using high-frequency administrative payroll data from countries with strong labor institutions (e.g., France, Germany) that exploit the timing of unanticipated minimum wage hikes (e.g., sudden political announcements or court rulings). — Such studies can directly test whether unanticipated changes amplify short-run unemployment fluctuations by comparing firm-level hiring/firing responses before and after the announcement, controlling for anticipated changes.

[PATH:theoretical] Search and matching models with firm-level uncertainty and staggered wage setting (e.g., extensions of the Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides framework) that incorporate the timing of minimum wage adjustments as a shock. — These models can simulate the differential employment effects of anticipated vs. unanticipated minimum wage changes, providing a theoretical mechanism for the amplification of unemployment fluctuations in regulated markets.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical literature on minimum wage and employment, focusing on studies that explicitly code the timing and anticipation of policy changes (e.g., Card & Krueger 1994 vs. more recent replication studies). — A systematic review can reveal whether the disputed relationship holds robustly across contexts, and whether unanticipated changes consistently yield larger short-run unemployment effects than anticipated ones.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching models with heterogeneous firms and wage rigidities, extended to incorporate staggered minimum wage adjustments and collective bargaining coverage. — A calibrated model can isolate the causal mechanism through which the timing of the minimum wage change (relative to labor market tightness) alters hiring and separation decisions, providing predictions that can be compared with empirical patterns.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing quasi-experimental studies on minimum wage effects in OECD countries, focusing on the timing of the policy change and the institutional context (e.g., collective bargaining coverage). — A systematic review can synthesize evidence on whether the timing of adjustments moderates short-run unemployment responses, and identify gaps or inconsistencies across studies to guide further research.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching models with heterogeneous firms and demand-driven business cycles (e.g., variations of the Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides framework) — Such models can formally derive conditions under which the timing of a wage floor shift relative to aggregate demand growth flips the sign of the employment response, providing a mechanism consistent with the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment effects that code the business cycle phase at implementation (e.g., updating Doucouliagos & Stanley, 2009) — A systematic review and meta-regression can identify whether studies that control for or condition on expansionary timing find systematically different short-run unemployment effects, directly testing the hypothesis across existing evidence.
